q.t: How long ago did Britain become permanently separated from the continent by the Channel?
q.e: For much of the Stone Age, Britain was connected to the continent by a land bridge. Britain only became permanently separated from the continent by the Channel about 10,000 years ago. The first farmers arrived in Britain about 6,000 years ago.

q.t: Which of these statements is correct?
q.e: Stonehenge, in what is now the English county of Wiltshire, was probably a special gathering place for seasonal ceremonies. Skara Brae on Orkney is the best preserved prehistoric village in northern Europe.
o: Skara Brae is the best preserved prehistoric village in northern Europe
Stonehenge is the best preserved prehistoric village in northern Europe

q.t: In which county is Stonehenge, and in which island group is Skara Brae?
q.e: One of these monuments, Stonehenge, still stands in what is now the English county of Wiltshire. Skara Brae on Orkney, off the north coast of Scotland, is the best preserved prehistoric village in northern Europe.
o: Stonehenge is in Wiltshire and Skara Brae is on Orkney
Stonehenge is in Dorset and Skara Brae is on Orkney
Stonehenge is in Wiltshire and Skara Brae is on Iona
Stonehenge is in Suffolk and Skara Brae is on Orkney

q.t: In the Bronze Age, what were the tombs in which people buried their dead called?
q.e: Around 4,000 years ago, people learned to make bronze. We call this period the Bronze Age. People lived in roundhouses and buried their dead in tombs called round barrows.

q.t: Where can a very impressive Iron Age hill fort still be seen?
q.e: People still lived in roundhouses, grouped together into larger settlements, and sometimes defended sites called hill forts. A very impressive hill fort can still be seen today at Maiden Castle, in the English county of Dorset.

q.t: To which language family did the language of the Iron Age people belong?
q.e: Most people were farmers, craft workers or warriors. The language they spoke was part of the Celtic language family. Similar languages were spoken across Europe in the Iron Age, and related languages are still spoken today in some parts of Wales, Scotland and Ireland.

q.t: Which TWO things did the Romans bring to Britain, according to the handbook?
q.e: The Romans remained in Britain for 400 years. They built roads and public buildings, created a structure of law, and introduced new plants and animals.

q.t: Who was Boudicca, and where is there a statue of her?
q.e: One of the tribal leaders who fought against the Romans was Boudicca, the queen of the Iceni in what is now eastern England. She is still remembered today and there is a statue of her on Westminster Bridge in London, near the Houses of Parliament.
o: Queen of the Iceni, with a statue on Westminster Bridge
Queen of the Picts, with a statue on Westminster Bridge
Queen of the Iceni, with a statue in Trafalgar Square
Queen of the Scots, with a statue on Westminster Bridge

q.t: Which TWO of these tribes invaded Britain from northern Europe after the Romans left?
q.e: Britain was again invaded by tribes from northern Europe: the Jutes, the Angles and the Saxons. The languages they spoke are the basis of modern-day English.

q.t: Which king united the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms in England and defeated the Vikings?
q.e: The Anglo-Saxon kingdoms in England united under King Alfred the Great, who defeated the Vikings. Many of the Viking invaders stayed in Britain, especially in the east and north of England, in an area known as the Danelaw.

q.t: Which TWO place names are given in the handbook as coming from the Viking languages?
q.e: Many of the Viking invaders stayed in Britain, especially in the east and north of England, in an area known as the Danelaw. Many place names there, such as Grimsby and Scunthorpe, come from the Viking languages.

q.t: Who was the first Danish king of England?
q.e: Anglo-Saxon kings continued to rule what is now England, except for a short period when there were Danish kings. The first of these was Cnut, also called Canute.

q.t: Under which king did the people of the north unite, leading to the term Scotland being used?
q.e: In the north, the threat of attack by Vikings had encouraged the people to unite under one king, Kenneth MacAlpin. The term Scotland began to be used to describe that country.

q.t: Which title did Henry VIII take in relation to Ireland?
q.e: Henry VII and Henry VIII had extended English control outside the Pale and had established English authority over the whole country. Henry VIII took the title 'King of Ireland'. English laws were introduced and local leaders were expected to follow the instructions of the Lord Lieutenants in Dublin.

q.t: What were the 'plantations' in Ireland?
q.e: The English government encouraged Scottish and English Protestants to settle in Ulster, the northern province of Ireland, taking over the land from Catholic landholders. These settlements were known as plantations. Many of the new settlers came from south-west Scotland.
o: Settlements of Scottish and English Protestants on land taken from Catholic landholders
Large farms growing potatoes for export
Forests planted to supply timber for the navy
Castles built to defend the Pale

q.t: Who mapped the coast of Australia during the period of increased colonisation?
q.e: This was also a time of increased colonisation overseas. Captain James Cook mapped the coast of Australia and a few colonies were established there. Britain gained control over Canada, and the East India Company, originally set up to trade, gained control of large parts of India.

q.t: What was the East India Company originally set up to do?
q.e: Britain gained control over Canada, and the East India Company, originally set up to trade, gained control of large parts of India. Colonies began to be established in southern Africa.
o: To map the coast of Australia

q.t: Which TWO goods came to Britain from North America and the West Indies?
q.e: Britain traded all over the world and began to import more goods. Sugar and tobacco came from North America and the West Indies; textiles, tea and spices came from India and the area that is today called Indonesia.

q.t: What was Richard Arkwright's original trade before he worked in textiles?
q.e: Born in 1732, Arkwright originally trained and worked as a barber. He was able to dye hair and make wigs. When wigs became less popular, he started to work in textiles. He improved the original carding machine.

q.t: What is carding, the process Arkwright's improved machine performed?
q.e: He improved the original carding machine. Carding is the process of preparing fibres for spinning into yarn and fabric. He also developed horse-driven spinning mills that used only one machine.
o: Preparing fibres for spinning into yarn and fabric
Weaving cloth on a mechanical loom
Dyeing wool before it is woven

q.t: What did Sake Dean Mahomet open in George Street, London in 1810?
q.e: In 1810 he opened the Hindoostane Coffee House in George Street, London. It was the first curry house to open in Britain. Mahomet and his wife also introduced 'shampooing', the Indian art of head massage, to Britain.
o: The Hindoostane Coffee House, the first curry house in Britain
The first Indian textile mill in Britain
The first cricket club in Britain
The first tennis club in Britain

q.t: Which process for the mass production of steel led to the development of shipbuilding and the railways?
q.e: The development of the Bessemer process for the mass production of steel led to the development of the shipbuilding industry and the railways. Manufacturing jobs became the main source of employment in Britain.

q.t: Against whom did Britain fight the Boer War, and where?
q.e: The Boer War of 1899 to 1902 made the discussions about the future of the Empire more urgent. The British went to war in South Africa with settlers from the Netherlands called the Boers. The Boers fought fiercely and the war went on for over three years.
o: Settlers from the Netherlands, in South Africa
Settlers from Germany, in South Africa
Settlers from the Netherlands, in Canada
Settlers from France, in South Africa

q.t: In which year was Rudyard Kipling awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature?
q.e: Rudyard Kipling was born in India in 1865 and later lived in India, the UK and the USA. His poems and novels reflected the idea that the British Empire was a force for good. Kipling was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1907.
